<reason>Both sides were competent and the clash stayed narrow and real: does historical demand expansion transfer when AI produces the cognitive output itself? PRO's sharpest work was the distinction that elasticity in output is not elasticity in labor when the same model fills extra volume, and the pointed pressure question about occupations with no liability sign-off. CON answered that pressure honestly (more localization volume, verification work scaling with output), and its ATM/spreadsheet pattern plus burden-of-proof framing was the strongest opposing material. However, two things tip this to PRO. First, CON's decisive closing attack — that PRO "quietly swapped 'will' for 'likely'" — misstates the proposition, which is explicitly framed as "likely"; PRO correctly flagged this, so CON's retreat narrative collapses. Second, CON conceded portable benefits and insurance are worth doing anyway, effectively giving away the policy prong while arguing only that timing should wait for indicators; PRO's lag argument (institutions take years, vacancies move after the freeze) was never squarely answered. CON's demand for a finished record of net decline is weak evidence given the rollout is early, and PRO exposed that. CON's answers were fluent, but its path to victory hinged on a misquoted motion and a partially conceded policy case. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question asking who restores headcount for copywriters, translators, and bookkeepers with no liability sign-off forced CON off the lawyer/liability ground, and CON's A1 answer (demand expansion in output volume, bookkeeping as the cleanest historical case) was strong — but PRO's Rebuttal 2 reply that CON's whole strategy is "raise the evidentiary bar until the disruption is already on the books," combined with catching CON treating the motion's "likely" as "will," was the exchange that decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
